title: Ahmed Muhaimin Choudhury
text: I am a data scientist in the making, currently in UBC’s Master of Data Science program. My path here ran through a Master’s in Economics, where a causal-impact study on COVID-19’s effect on Bangladesh’s macroeconomy first pulled me toward the field. Before circling back to it, I spent seven years as a creative director in Bangladeshi advertising, learning how to turn complexity into things people actually understand. That combination is what I bring: quantitative rigour with the communication craft to match. Long-term, I am drawn to high-stakes, data-rich domains like energy markets, healthcare analytics, and derivatives, where good models change real decisions and clear explanations of them are rare.

title: My first weeks in MDS
text:
I got to Canada a month before the program started and spent it in Calgary with my wife, easing into the country before easing into the degree. We spent our anniversary glamping in Kananaskis, drove up to Banff, and I picked up paddleboarding on Bow Lake, Barrier Lake, and a handful of others whose names I’ve already lost. I flew into Vancouver the day before orientation, which in hindsight was cutting it close, but I’d wanted every last day of that Alberta stretch. My first impression of UBC is that I would not want to leave in ten months. I’ve been slowly working my way through it since, the Museum of Anthropology, Tower Beach, the Rose Garden, Nitobe, all of it quietly making the case that this was the right choice.
Orientation was the fun part. Somewhere between the icebreakers and the campus goose chase, I stopped feeling like the new guy and started feeling like part of a cohort. A lot of the pep talks were built around how to survive the program, which was a strange note to open on given that most of us were already plenty scared, but I got to meet people, had fun explaining how to pronounce my name, and run around the campus with my team on the goose chase. There was also a running theme of warnings about how depressing Vancouver gets in winter. Jury’s still out.
Then week one arrived and we were thrown straight onto the roller coaster tracks. Not even the seats, just the tracks. We’ve been zooming past labs and worksheets ever since. The workload is genuinely intense, but the trauma bonding it produces is more intense still, and it’s been wonderful to see how many different paths and peole have crossed their paths here. I’m overwhelmed, I haven’t seen the inside of a gym since I got here, and I’m trying to keep my head above water long enough to actually enjoy what I signed up for. I’ve got ten months to figure out what I’m doing, ace the next quiz, and build something I’m proud of. That’s the plan for now.



When life was still flowery

title: About
text: I grew up in Dhaka, obsessed with science fiction and convinced I’d become a scientist who built robots and brain microchips that can copy paste skills. Life took a longer route. In grade 6 I started competitive debating, and the questions that stuck with me were the ones about economics: why do things work the way they do in an underdeveloped country, and who gets to decide. That pulled me toward studying economics, first at BRAC University, then a Master’s at North South University, where my thesis used a causal-impact model employing Bayesian structural time series to estimate how COVID-19 affected Bangladesh’s macroeconomy. The finding I could stand behind was a significant increase in foreign reserves. The rest of the results didn’t survive their p-values, and I learned early how honest data work has to be with itself.

title: About
text:
From advertising to data science
Somewhere along the way I also fell in love with writing, so after graduation I spent seven years as a copywriter and creative manager at Asiatic MCL, the largest agency in Bangladesh. My clients included BRAC, Unilever, GSK, PepsiCo, Airtel, Toffee, USAID, and UKAID, among about fifty others. The work I’m proudest of came at the start of the pandemic: a joint project with BRAC and USAID where we built a rumour map of Bangladesh, tracking which misinformation was spreading in which districts, and then produced the TVCs, billboards, and targeted digital work to counter it. It was the first time I saw data and communication saving lives in the same breath.

title: About
text:
Why data science
The pivot started there and finished during my master’s thesis, where R stopped being a tool and became a way of thinking. In advertising I built arguments from cultural insight. I want to build them from evidence I can defend line by line. I sat in enough boardrooms watching decisions turn on a chart no one felt qualified to question, and I got tired of being on the wrong side of that asymmetry. Data science is how I plan to close it, for myself and eventually for the teams and organisations I work with. UBC MDS is where I’m starting, because the program is built for people who care more about problems than about pedigree, and because learning in an environment tied to industry is how I know I learn best.

title: About
text:
Outside of data science
Weekends usually mean poker with friends, paddleboarding (something I picked up recently and can’t get enough of), or a good film. I’ll take a thriller, a crime story, sci-fi, or a slow drama, in any order. When none of that fits the mood, I disappear into a passion project and vibe-code my way through it until the sun is up. I play the guitar and love grunge, hip hop, and metal, though Murakami on the shelf and a FIFA session on the couch balance things out. I cook a killer khichuri and biryani, and if you’ve had my milk tea you already know. Right now I’m learning Japanese and French, studying chess seriously enough to lose sleep over it, and building the courage to try learning skydiving and scuba diving within the next year. I love writing poems and making short reels which are small love letters to the life I have and all the amazing git people in it.

title: Can Flipper Length be used to identify Penguin Species?

Data: Palmer Penguins, Palmer Station Antarctica LTER, released under CC0.
For this post, I will be applying some newfound skills in Python to do a little analysis on the Palmer Penguins dataset.

title: Can Flipper Length be used to identify Penguin Species?
text:
Data

from palmerpenguins import load_penguins
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

penguins = load_penguins().dropna(subset=["flipper_length_mm", "species"])

The Palmer Penguins dataset records measurements from 344 penguins across three species (Adelie, Chinstrap, Gentoo) sampled at Palmer Station, Antarctica. This post looks at one measurement: flipper length.

title: Can Flipper Length be used to identify Penguin Species?
text:
Summary

summary = (
    penguins
    .groupby("species")["flipper_length_mm"]
    .agg(["mean", "median", "std", "min", "max", "count"])
    .round(1)
)

Based on flipper length, the three species differ noticeably. Adelie penguins have the shortest flippers on average, Chinstraps sit in the middle, and Gentoos are clearly the largest.

title: Can Flipper Length be used to identify Penguin Species?
text:
Visualization

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4.5))
species_order = ["Adelie", "Chinstrap", "Gentoo"]
data = [penguins.loc[penguins["species"] == s, "flipper_length_mm"] for s in species_order]

ax.boxplot(data, label=species_order, patch_artist=True)
ax.set_ylabel("Flipper length (mm)")
ax.set_xlabel("Species")
ax.grid(axis="y", alpha=0.3)
plt.show()







Figure 1: Flipper length distribution by penguin species. Gentoo penguins have the longest flippers by a wide margin.

title: Can Flipper Length be used to identify Penguin Species?
text:
Inference
From the figure, it’s evident that the gap between Gentoo and the other two species is large enough that flipper length alone would be a decent classifier for that species particularly. Adelie and Chinstrap overlap considerably in flipper length, so distinguishing between those two would need additional features than flipper length.

title: Do Manual Cars Really Pack More Horsepower?
text:
Data: mtcars, extracted from the 1974 Motor Trend US magazine and bundled with base R. See ?mtcars for the full variable list. Public domain.
For ages, stick car people have taunted the automatic car users like they don’t qualify to be on their level. And no one actually questioned, who’s faster? Who packs more horsepower? I am looking for an answer to that question today. Today, is the day of revelation.

title: Do Manual Cars Really Pack More Horsepower?
text:
Data

library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

cars <- mtcars |>
  mutate(transmission = if_else(am == 0, "Automatic", "Manual"))

The mtcars dataset records fuel consumption and ten aspects of automobile design and performance for 32 cars from the 1973–74 model year. This post asks one question: Do manual-transmission cars tend to have more horsepower than automatic ones?

title: Do Manual Cars Really Pack More Horsepower?
text:
Summary



Table 1: Summary statistics of horsepower across both types of transmissions in cars.


cars |>
  group_by(transmission) |>
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    mean_hp = round(mean(hp), 1),
    median_hp = round(median(hp), 1),
    sd_hp = round(sd(hp), 1),
    min_hp = min(hp),
    max_hp = max(hp)
  )

# A tibble: 2 × 7
  transmission     n mean_hp median_hp sd_hp min_hp max_hp
  <chr>        <int>   <dbl>     <dbl> <dbl>  <dbl>  <dbl>
1 Automatic       19    160.       175  53.9     62    245
2 Manual          13    127.       109  84.1     52    335




Automatic cars in this dataset actually have a higher mean horsepower than manual cars, but the standard deviation is large and the sample size is small. The distribution matters more than the mean.

title: Do Manual Cars Really Pack More Horsepower?
text:
Visualization

ggplot(cars, aes(x = hp, fill = transmission)) +
  geom_density(alpha = 0.5) +
  labs(
    x = "Horsepower",
    y = "Density",
    fill = "Transmission"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()







Figure 1: Density of horsepower by transmission type. Automatic cars show a heavier right tail, while manual cars cluster more tightly at the lower end.

title: Do Manual Cars Really Pack More Horsepower?
text:
Inference
The density plot tells a more nuanced story than the summary means. Manual cars concentrate in the 60–130 hp range, whereas automatics are more spread out and include a heavier right tail up past 300 hp. The perception that “manuals are always sportier” doesn’t hold in this dataset as it’s the automatics that carry the high-horsepower muscle cars of the mid-1970s. A larger, more modern sample would probably flip the story, but for 1974 Motor Trend cars, automatic transmission and high horsepower go together more often than not.
